title: Implementation
intro: The shelf runs except for four marked gaps, two in the Python API and two in the TypeScript page. Make the backlog's rules true in both.
taskPanel:
Implementation: fill the marked gaps

The shelf runs except for four marked gaps: two in the Python API (api/shelf.py: books and lend) and two in the TypeScript page (web/src/lib/shelf.ts: shelfLabel and sortForShelf). Make the backlog's rules true in both layers.

What good looks like

- books lists by title ignoring case, then id, and the author filter ignores case and surrounding spaces.
- lend refuses an unknown id, a blank borrower, and a book already on loan.
- shelfLabel and sortForShelf agree with the API about what a person reads.
- The visible tests pass before you submit; the hidden suites ask more.

Using the AI mentor well

Paste the failing test's name, not your whole file, and ask what rule it is checking. The mentor explains; it does not write the function for you.
objectives: Implement books with the author filter and shelf order (SH-1)
Implement shelfLabel so a lent book says so (SH-4)
Implement sortForShelf so the page agrees with the API (SH-1)

criteria.title: Correctness (hidden tests)
criteria.description: The sealed suites, one per layer, ask the same rules many more questions.

criteria.title: Visible tests
criteria.description: The suites you can see pass, and you can run them before submitting.

criteria.title: Code quality
criteria.description: No TODO left behind, reasonable complexity, docstrings kept.

criteria.title: Process
criteria.description: You ran the tests before submitting and used the mentor in moderation.

assistant.systemPrompt: You are the LearnSDLC mentor for the IMPLEMENTATION phase of Shelf, a teacher's own application: a Python Flask API that keeps books in memory and a TypeScript React page that lists them. The learner completes books and lend in api/shelf.py and shelfLabel and sortForShelf in web/src/lib/shelf.ts. Explain concepts and ask guiding questions; never write the learner's answer for them. Keep replies under 120 words and end with one question.

hints: Which two decisions does books make, and in which order should it make them?
What key would make two books with the same title keep a stable order?
Which three things can make a loan impossible, and which exception does the route expect for each?
Read give_back just below: what does it check first?
What does a person read on one line, and which part depends on the year?
Does sort change the array it is called on? What does the docstring promise?

progressive: Run the visible tests first and read which rule each failing case names.
Do the Python gaps, then the TypeScript ones: the rules are the same.
Run both suites again before you submit; the hidden suites add the edge cases.
